cards.text: Jacob, Isaac's son, has been working for Laban, his father-in-law. Rachel, one of Jacob's wives, has just given birth to a son named Joseph. Right after that, Jacob walks up to Laban with something on his mind.

cards.question: Jacob has something to ask his father-in-law Laban. What is it?

answers.text: Send him on his way back home
Give him a field of his own
Let him build a house nearby

cards.question: Jacob plans to leave his wives and children behind with Laban and go home alone.

cards.text: Laban is NOT ready to let him go. He says, "If I have found favor in your eyes, please stay."

cards.question: Laban says he has learned by divination that the LORD has ___ him because of Jacob.

cards.text: Then Laban says, "Name your wages, and I will pay them." Friend, when the boss says NAME YOUR PRICE, you don't blink, you don't cough, you don't check your phone. You start TALKING.
And Jacob talks. He reminds Laban how he has served him and how Laban's livestock have thrived under his care.

cards.question: Jacob tells Laban that he had very little before Jacob arrived, but now his wealth has increased many times over.

cards.text: Then Jacob asks, "But now, when may I also provide for my own household?" And Laban asks, "What can I give you?"

cards.question: Jacob says Laban doesn't need to give him anything. He'll keep shepherding Laban's flocks if Laban does one thing. What does Jacob want as his wages?

answers.text: The strongest rams in the flock
A tenth of every new lamb

cards.question: Jacob says his ___ will testify for him when Laban comes to check on his wages in the future.

cards.text: Jacob even spells it out: any goat of his that isn't speckled or spotted, or any lamb that isn't dark-colored, will be considered stolen. That's a man signing his name in PERMANENT MARKER.

cards.question: After hearing all that, Laban turns down Jacob's offer.

cards.text: Laban agreed, and he does NOT waste time. That very day, Laban himself removes every streaked, speckled or spotted goat, every one with any white on it, and every dark-colored lamb.

cards.question: Laban has pulled all the spotted and dark-colored animals out of the flocks. Whose care does he put them under?
Then Laban puts a ___ journey between himself and Jacob.

cards.text: So Jacob keeps shepherding the rest of Laban's flocks. Then he grabs fresh branches of poplar, almond and plane trees and starts peeling off the bark, one branch at a time, like a man with a PLAN.

cards.question: Jacob peels the bark off the fresh branches. What does that leave showing?
Where does Jacob set the peeled branches, right in front of the flocks?

answers.text: Along the path to the field

cards.text: When the flocks are in heat and come to drink, they mate right there in front of those branches.

cards.question: The young the flocks bear come out streaked or speckled or spotted.

cards.text: Jacob sets those young apart. Then he makes the rest of the flock face the streaked dark-colored sheep in Laban's flocks.

cards.question: Jacob keeps his own stock mixed in with Laban's animals.

cards.text: And now Jacob gets PICKY. Whenever the stronger females are in heat, he puts the branches in the troughs, in full view, so they'll breed in front of them.

cards.question: If the animals were ___, Jacob did not set out the branches.
So the stronger animals go to Jacob, and the weaker ones go to Laban.
So how does all of this turn out for Jacob?

answers.text: He loses most of his flocks

cards.text: Large flocks, maidservants and menservants, camels AND donkeys. The man who asked when he could provide for his own household just got his answer, and trust me, friend, this story is NOT done.

findings.problem: Genesis 30:25 says only that Jacob spoke to Laban 'after Rachel had given birth to Joseph.' The card adds immediacy that the text doesn't give: 'has just given birth' and 'Right after that.'

rule.text: Times stay true. No time in the text means none added.

findings.problem: The opening card states facts from outside the passage: Jacob is Isaac's son, Laban is his father-in-law, and Rachel is one of his wives (Genesis 25, 29). The card cites only Genesis 30:25. The docs say outside facts come 'with their reference,' but they also say a story card cites only the verses it tells, 'no wider and no narrower.' They don't say how a card cites an outside fact.
findings.question: When a story card uses a fact from outside the passage, such as who a person is, should the outside reference be cited? If so, where should it go, given that the card's verses field must cover only the verses it tells?

findings.problem: This story card has three sentences: the Laban quote, the 'Friend, when the boss says...' line and 'You start TALKING.' Story cards other than the opening card are limited to 1 to 2 sentences.

rule.text: Every other story card is 1 to 2 sentences.

findings.problem: 'So Jacob keeps shepherding the rest of Laban's flocks' makes it sound like Jacob keeps shepherding because Laban moved away. Genesis 30:36 only says Laban moved away 'while Jacob was shepherding.' The text doesn't connect the two.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'He becomes exceedingly prosperous,' uses the BSB's own wording ('exceedingly'). That makes it sound more like the Bible than the plain wrong answers, 'He loses most of his flocks' and 'He ends up owing Laban,' so it stands out.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.
